title: Why Go exists: fast compilation, a single binary and simplicity

videos.script: This is the first lesson of the course, and it writes almost no code. It answers a question instead: why does Go exist at all? {{google}} In 2007, three engineers at Google were tired of waiting. One of their C++ programs took forty-five minutes to build. Their servers had many processors and spent the day on the network, and the languages they used were designed before either was normal. {{build}} Go was their answer, and here you measure it. The go command is itself a Go program. It builds from nothing, more than three hundred packages, in under half a minute. {{binary}} Then the thing Go hands you at the end: one file. You copy it to another Linux machine and it runs, with nothing to install first. The same source builds for Windows and for a Mac without leaving this one. {{keywords}} Last, what the designers left out on purpose. No classes, no exceptions, no conversions you did not ask for. A short program counts the keywords of the whole language, and there are twenty-five. {{close}} Lesson 2 tells the story from 2009 to the version you are running.
